title: Should you still learn programming if AI can code?
author: KwonDarko

comments.author: Jaded_Software_
comments.body: No, learn infrastructure, data design, and architecture. Nobody learns how to write assembly anymore, code is going the same way.

replies.author: Strange-Tap5860
replies.body:
Do you really think someone can learn those things without ever needing to code? I think that is impossible.

A.I is already decent at all that stuff anyway. Next year it will be bettee than humans at it.

replies.author: Relevant-Positive-48
replies.body: It is 100% not true that "Nobody learns how to write assembly anymore".  The vast majority of people never use it in production but a good number of CS programs still teach it - either explicitly or as part of systems programming and/or systems architecture courses.  It's amazing for understanding how the computer works.

replies.author: ffxivthrowaway03
replies.body: Yeah, that's like saying "don't learn algebra because a calculator can do it."  You need to have at least a functional understanding of how it works in order to use the calculator *correctly.*

replies.author: Jaded_Software_
replies.body:
Sure, I took assembly in undergrad and then never used it again.

But, I think if the goal is to just be a Game Dev, I would say that learning code is a waste of time. You’re better letting Claude handle the code and learn how to properly debug your game in the engine, and then how to properly describe those to a Claude.

replies.author: _raydeStar
replies.body: If you interview for an SWE position, they will still put you in front of a whiteboard and ask you to code.  I check every few months.  because algorithms is now my weakest subject lol -- gotta still grind leetcode.

replies.author: roodammy44
replies.body:
It’s a bad comparison.

With a compiler you are 99.99999% certain that the instruction you gave the compiler results in the right code being generated in assembly.

With AI I would give it right now an 85% trust rating.

That’s fine if you’re writing a game or some piece of code not on the critical path. But it’s not good enough for most uses of code out there, hence why code reviews and demand for senior engineers is still there.

comments.author: Least-Inevitable7146
comments.body:
2 years ago I would have say he's right, keep learning even now I'm wondering, if everybody stop learning it, what will happen in the next few years. But the thing is, Will smith eating pasta with stable diffusion is the same as AI regarding coding. It was ugly, now we barely have a good image with opus 5.5 but in two of three years we can have a all movie.

Ai is getting useful and smarter very fast. So now, I'm still wondering if it's worth learning to get a job for New juniors. Or just learn how to really use codex, Claude cli, understand token, architecture, how to design a system etc.

The new coding might be the design architecture itself and the tools around it. Not the language anymore.

comments.author: angrykirby
comments.body: for now yes do you want to spend 3 hours telling it to move a button that's in the wrong place or do you want to just go into the code and edit the JavaScript yourself in 5 seconds it's worth learning some coding I don't think you're going to have to master it like you used to but there are things that like your AI will get caught up on that you can do in 3 seconds so yes for now anyway

replies.author: ItsDumi
replies.body:
Exactly this. I've been prompting code but typing it all out myself AND reading the JS manual. Literally disallowing myself from copy paste unless it's CSS (vause im gonna do a huge ui rework anyway). In a month I've learnt a shit load because, from what I've seen, a lot of learning to code is writing the same syntax so much you remember how to use it. 

Understanding how your systems work and communicate is so damn important I can't stress it enough

comments.author: poundofcake
comments.body: Learn concepts.

replies.author: Relevant-Positive-48
replies.body:
This!  Learning the concepts makes learning languages easier.

Learning programming well is a tried and true access to learning concepts but it is the concepts that are key.

comments.author: Correct_Emotion8437
comments.body: I think it’s super helpful to know one language well.  It teaches you a lot of the concepts you need to know and allows you to read code.  I can read code in any language (that I’ve tried) even though I only write in one.

comments.author: Ball_Analytics
comments.body: Personally think that's my advantage. Leads to a lot of You're right replies which infuriate me but you can't point out what's wrong without knowing where to point. Plus optimization should be the aim, pure vibecoding never does... in a sense the LLM is like a dog, it's not sitting because you asked it sit, its sitting because its expects a treat.

comments.author: johnesco
comments.body: You can make games without coding, but at this time, knowing zero code, even while vibe coding, puts you at a disadvantage. Knowing at least some basic code and how code is moved and managed and deployed is still very important. Understanding the heart of data structures, a bit about memory, and why bigO notation exists.

comments.author: mirageofstars
comments.body: I think it’s better to learn how to design, plan, and assess from a product perspective.

comments.author: Novaworld7
comments.body:
I see both sides here and I think I land in the middle. It's important to be able to read the code, follow the code, and understand it if you choose to look at it. 

I don't think you need to know how to code, that's something entirely different. However, you do need to know the terms for what you are trying to do and you do need to know the right tools (more or less) for the job. 

In my experience, the best way is to set yourself up for a few projects and work through them. For example try to spin up a discord clone, that will hit so many boxes, make a ticketing system, make obsidian all over again. Picking a few of these will expose you to different things and you'll ask why this or why that and eventually you'll start to learn the terms. 

Your prompts will get better, you'll do less tear downs, etc.

comments.author: RoboProletariat
comments.body: If you are letting the AI do 100% of the work, then you are just a user playing with a toy.

comments.body: As shit like AGENTS.MD files get more complex and bloated with more and more markdown files being included . . . "AI first coding" is starting to dip into an uncanny valley of a . . . I dunno, extremely weakly typed pythtml with a middleman compiler that takes a half an hour and does good job of really capturing the LGTM work you turn in on a friday?

comments.author: Apocaloid
comments.body: Did engineering go away when machines became automated? Who's going to push the frontier of AI? Go for the science of computers, not so much the trade.

comments.author: redosabe
comments.body: Should I learn to do math if a calculator can do it?

comments.author: r0b0c0p87
comments.body: I wouldn't, just like I wouldn't learn to churn butter, but if someone wanted to learn it as a hobby, I wouldn't fault them for it.

replies.author: DrinkingAtQuarks
replies.body: Have you ever tried hand churned butter? It's outrageously good compared to the supermarket stuff.

comments.author: zenmatrix83
comments.body: Do you need a masters in programming no, should you know something yes. The bigger a project gets the more likely you’ll run out of issues , as agents still lose stuff and start guess about thinks outside of what fits in its context

comments.author: JimboTheBurninator
comments.body: Since 2026 LLMs got this good I do projects where I choose not to look at the code and don't worry about the architecture either. But I have other projects where I'm deeply in the architecture of the codebase because the LLM is making terrible choices without my involvement. In that case learning to WRITE code doesn't matter, but I still need to understand all of it.

comments.author: chaicpp
comments.body:
If you're living rent-free, working on your own, or have infinite free-time, you can ride the industry shift until reading code isn't needed. 

However, if you have to work and need an edge, it's very important to understand the code. I'm telling you this out of experience. I've been writing code for a long time so code isn't a foreign language for me. I actually have an opinion and suggestions regarding the generated code.

But in general, I think it's more important learning how to take a product to market, planning, infrastructure (for online games), designing robust systems. All the technical work will get done by agents. Focus on making a good game, get good at that. **Game Design**.

Most importantly, if possible remove the dependency of an 8 hour job as quick as possible. Easier said than done, but the quicker you're on your own, the better. 

Btw, I'm not saying to quit your job if you have one. Work on your own thing asap is what I'm saying.

comments.author: haaheehachoo
comments.body: Yeah learn the basics. If you don’t know what types, loops, ifs, functions, classes are, you’ll be on shaky ground as a dev.

comments.author: Disastrous-Gain5870
comments.body: It’s a waste of time at this point. Very soon AI will be better at coding than any living human. It’s arguable to say it already is.

comments.author: Calm-Phrase-382
comments.body: I think you should. It’s still beneficial to understand algorithms, data structures, computer architecture, at least the 101. I use ai to code, and don’t write much, just review, and there’s things the ai is doing that I catch that arnt necessarily bad, but don’t match overall scope of the project. I ofc don’t do like a one prompt design. If you want to develop software, 100% knowing the fundamentals of computer science will absolutely increase the quality of your work, there’s no downside.
